articleTitle: Petri net applications: Modeling software, hardware, and other systems with this powerful tool
abstract: As mentioned in “Petrinets,” on page 18, Petrinets can be extremely useful as models. They are a powerful tool in studying the response and dynamic qualities of concurrent, asynchronous, and synchronized systems. In this article, we will discuss modeling computer software, hardware, and other systems. Also, the various analysis techniques and extensions of Petri nets will be discussed.

articleTitle: Of birds, bees, and airplanes: Technology can take lessons from nature on how to produce flying machines
abstract: Atiny monarch butterfly can migrate south 3000 kilometers to the grove of trees in central Mexico from which its great-great-grandparents started north some eight months earlier. It has the genetically-derived instinct to perform the mission without outside guidance, and the senses and intellect to navigate, adapt to meteorological conditions, and avoid predators. A giant airliner can perform a similar transportation task for hundreds of human travelers, using the structure and muscle of aeronautical engineering, and navigational mechanisms interacting with human management. Each of these flying creations represents an elegant design superbly adapted to its mission.

articleTitle: Biomolecular information processing: Biotechnology paves the way for new approaches to computing
abstract: In the nineteenth century, the synthesis of the biological compound urea by organic chemists established that living organisms were not always necessary to produce organic materials. Today, the challenge is to use organic materials to form a molecular computer that can process information in a lifelike manner. The desire to do so stems in part from important and difficult problems that face today's computer scientist. Three of the most challenging areas are effective pattern recognition in ambiguous environments, efficient utilization of parallelism, and learning from experience.

articleTitle: Expert systems in space: Minimizing crew and ground support with knowledge-based systems at Marshall Space Flight Center
abstract: As the electrical power requirements for spacecraft increase, the complexity of managing such systems also increases. A key lesson learned from the first American space station, Skylab, was that future spacecraft with larger power systems must minimize ground support and crew involvement.

articleTitle: Personally, I like PCs: TK!Solver software, and the right user can produce amazing results
abstract: Dear Dad, please send money for a personal computer. The engineering curriculum is tough enough without relying on tools of a bygone age …

articleTitle: Antennas for satellites: Around the world with antennas made for three-axis stabilized spacecraft
abstract: Every satellite in orbit carries one or more antennas whose characteristics are determined by the coverage requirements of its communications system. There are dozens of surveillance and remote sensing satellites in low earth orbit (LEO), at altitudes less than approximately 2500 km. These satellites see an ever-changing land or seascape. There are also dozens of satellites designed specifically for communications and TV broadcast service. Most of the latter are in a 24-hour geosynchronous orbit (GEO) at 35,800 km altitude so that the satellite sees an apparently stationary earth beneath it. In between LEO and GEO, an important constellation of satellites in 12-hour orbits (20,200 km altitude) is emerging. These are the Navstar satellites of the Global Positioning System (GPS), designed to broadcast precise navigational information to both military and commercial users anywhere on earth.

articleTitle: Hybrid optical computing: High accuracy, high data rate, electro-optical architecture
abstract: Lightweight and pocket sized, the optical signal processor can perform a myriad of complicated processing operations. Its success is primarily due to the profound diffraction phenomena of coherent light. The essential merit of an optical signal processor is its capability to process a signal in complex amplitude, parallelism, large capacity, high speed and diversified wavelength. Several processing operations have proven to be more efficient with optical techniques than with their electronic counterparts. These operations are: Fourier transforms, convolutions, correlation operations and spectrum analysis. The major advantages of an electronic computer is its flexibility, programmability and easy accessability. (Optical signal processors are very inflexible compared with electronic computers.) The question is, “Can we exploit the efficient operation of optics and the flexibility of electronics to come up with a realistic electro-optical (EO) architecture that meets our computational needs?” The answer to this question is, “yes.”

articleTitle: Automotive electronics: Improved safety, handling, emission, and audio-visual technologies for the car of the future
abstract: Recently, automotive technology has made great strides by applying electronics to the design process. Even more innovations are anticipated in the near future. Electronics provide important car control and communications features that were previously either impossible or too costly to implement. The growth of the consumer electronics market, including high-quality entertainment systems, electronic display devices, and two-way radio communicators, has raised a strong public demand for electronically-equipped automobiles. Furthermore, technological advances are bringing these products into the automobile in a cost-effective manner.

articleTitle: Petri nets: An examination of a versatile modeling tool
abstract: To study the response and dynamic properties of engineering systems — or any other natural science systems — using a model helps. It is useful not only in representing and describing the system, but also offers a flexible mathematical view for acquiring new knowledge or ideas about the systems.

articleTitle: Measurements in nondestructive evaluation: An interdisciplinary subject dedicated to understanding flaws and failures
abstract: In man's continuing efforts to build better machines, it has become increasingly clear that we must put more effort into the safety and reliability of the machines. A relatively new discipline, especially to electrical and computer engineers, is the area of Nondestructive Evaluation (NDE). NDE is dedicated to understanding the measurement of flaws and the failure of materials. It is an interdisciplinary subject which draws upon physics, metallurgy, and many engineering areas. For engineers who like to incorporate a variety of experimental and theoretical techniques into their work, NDE provides a rigorous challenge.

articleTitle: Microelectronic fabrication: An examination of the ever growing struggle to get smaller
abstract: Microelectronics, the science and art of electronic miniaturization, is a field full of excitement, challenge and rapid change. The first successful planar fabrication techniques produced single transistors in 1959, and integrated circuits were fabricated shortly thereafter at Fair-child Semiconductor and Texas Instruments. These first integrated circuits formed simple logic gates from several transistors and resistors. From this modest beginning, the number of electronic components on an integrated circuits die doubled yearly through the mid 1970s as shown in Fig. 1. Since then, the growth rate appears to have decreased to one of quadrupling every three years.

articleTitle: Recognizing the parallelism of data-flow: Many computer architectures expedite parallel processing
abstract: With technology approaching the limits of semiconductor speeds, computer scientists search for other ways to meet the processing demands of more sophisticated applications. Real-time processing, artificial intelligence, and distributed systems have each triggered computer architectures suited to their individual needs. The expectation of general purpose machines may give way to very dedicated systems. Common to these new designs, though, is the exploitation of parallel processing.

articleTitle: Parts obsolescence: A new concern for EEs: Microcircuits you plan to use today may not be available tomorrow
abstract: The technologies for electronic microcircuits have evolved rapidly over the past 20 years. But an explosion has occurred in the 1980s. Semiconductor houses have stopped making many parts that were designed just a few years ago. As a result, parts obsolescence problems in the microcircuit arena are mounting up to millions of dollars to groups such as the military services. But why should this be of concern to you? Aren't semiconductor houses providing engineering schools with the latest technology parts? No. The senior projects you are working on and the designs you are becoming comfortable with may include technology up to three years old. By the time you design your first electronic circuit for industry the microcircuits you specify may be obsolete. We have seen it happen.

articleTitle: Proliferating hospital testing devices: Too much monitoring could be hazardous to a patient's health
abstract: The rapid development of instruments for use in hospitals and clinics has created problems in various areas of the medical field. The majority of these problems are caused by the large number of instruments used. Physically, the mass or mess of cables and tubes can be confusing, be hard to untangle, and require patience. The number of alarms that could ring at any time are very intimidating and difficult to distinguish from one another. The overlapping of information given by the instruments often seems to waste time and also adds to the confusion.

articleTitle: Looking for extraterrestrial life: The search is for societies that are willing to join the club
abstract: People have always wondered whether there are other people. Chosen from innumerable quotes that could be adduced, from classical Greek times to the nineteenth century, here is the thought of Teng Mu, Chinese philosopher of the thirteenth century, “Empty space is like a kingdom, and heaven and earth no more than a single individual person in that kingdom. Upon one tree are many fruits, and in one kingdom many people. How unreasonable it would be to suppose that, besides the heavens and earth which we can see, there are no other heavens and no other earths?”

articleTitle: The EE as naval officer: Now more than ever the U.S. Navy has a lot to offer the undergrad and grad
abstract: The United States bases a significant portion of its defense strategy on advanced technology. Thus, the need is obvious for technically qualified personnel to design, evaluate, and operate the vast array of equipment that supports the national defense.

articleTitle: Looking back
APL: Dramatically reduce coding time on your PC with this powerful language
abstract: Have you ever felt it would be nice to write a computer program to solve a special problem, but the time required to do so was not justified? You were probably right if you were thinking in terms of BASIC, FORTRAN or C. The thoughts of data declarations, specifying array dimensions and nested loops to process those arrays are sufficient to deter anyone whose time is valuable.

articleTitle: The strategic defense initiative: An innovative science and technology perspective that's much more than “star wars”
abstract: The Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) proposed by President Reagan immediately caught the fancy of the news media who dubbed it the “Star Wars Program.” However, only in the fantasy world of films can the tasks envisioned by the program be accomplished by a few swashbuckling space heroes who take on all the technological might of an evil empire and succeed. By contrast, the SDI program goals will require a major commitment of scientific assets, money, and people just to establish feasibility of the concepts.

articleTitle: What happens to the other 75 percent? A case study of one university's findings on GPA statistics versus job opportunities
abstract: Interfacing with industries interested in our graduates is one of the enjoyable aspects of teaching. Typically, all the parties share a sincere desire to be as helpful to each other as possible, along with a shared concern for the future welfare of the graduating students. This attitude of mutual good will is especially apparent in recruitment representatives who are proud of their companies. Occasionally, however, a recruiter, new on the circuit, allows his pride in his company to reach such a high level that he drops a comment like, “We would like to talk to your best students.” Or even the somewhat more conservative, “We would like to interview your top 25 percent.” We suspect, though, that this thought occurs many more times than it is openly stated. This led to the question which became the basis of our study, “What happens to the other 75 percent?”

articleTitle: Continuing education equals technical vitality: For today's dynamic engineer commencement does not mark the end of one's formal education
abstract: The goal of continuing education is not only to maintain and increase skills; vitality is the broader goal. Vitality is the foundation for career success; it is the intellectual vigor, the creativity, and the diligence with which professional tasks are initiated, pursued, and completed. Remaining vital is a strong contributor to increased job satisfaction and to greater job security.

articleTitle: Electrical engineering and the computer: A look at the practical uses of computer modeling in industry and academe
abstract: The evolving saga of the computer/information revolution is a fascinating one. Raw computer power alone has increased by a factor of approximately a million (from ~ 1,000 to ~ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">9</sup> Floating-point Operations per Second or FLOPS) between the introduction of the UNIVAC-1 (about 1953) and the CRAY-2 (about 1986). Along with this speed increase have come similar improvements in highspeed memory (from ~ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup> to ~ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sup> bits), and input/output speed (from ~ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> to ~ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sup> bits/sec). There is no other area of human activity where comparable advances have occurred in the same time frame.

articleTitle: Looking back
Opportunities in computer engineering: Your questions about this dynamic area of specialization are answered
abstract: “What is computer engineering? What is the difference between computer engineering and computer science? What is the difference between electrical engineering and computer engineering? Why study computer engineering? What computer engineering programs are available in the U.S.? What opportunities are there after graduation? How much does a computer engineer get paid?”

articleTitle: Biomedical engineering: The struggle to prolong quality life: While not perfected, the artificial heart is a symbol of great things to come
abstract: William Schroeder's dream of living an additional ten years with his Jarvik-7 artificial heart did not come true. He died of a massive stroke in August 1986, less than two years after implantation. Although he survived a record 620 days, longer than way of the animals who received artificial hearts in early experiments, he endured a seesaw ordeal. He suffered a series of strokes which left him partially paralyzed and impaired, but his family's support as well as his own sense of humor and perseverance, helped him fight back.

articleTitle: Breaking the frequency barrier: Hearing aids based on digital signal processing and VLSI technology
abstract: Roughly 27 million Americans have some measurable hearing loss, but only 16 million have a deficiency severe enough to affect them in a noticeable way. Sensorineural loss, the most common hearing deficiency, results primarily from the intensity of various damaging noises the ears have been subjected to over the years. The loss is often partial affecting only certain frequencies perceived by the ear such as the higher frequencies of women's and children's voices.

articleTitle: Branch involvement: Rewarding and fun: CSU — Chico student branch demonstrates how it is done
abstract: Each spring at California State University at Chico (CSUC) a week long celebration is held commemorating the pioneering figures of this country since the turn of the century. Fraternities, sororities, and other campus organizations participate in various activities throughout the week known as Pioneer Days. The festivities are culminated with a parade which is the second largest annually held parade in California. (The Rose parade is the largest.) The 1986 Pioneer Days marked the first time an IEEE Student Branch at CSUC has entered a float in this parade.

articleTitle: Saving for that first job: The key to financial success after graduation is smart planning
abstract: Looking forward to graduating next spring? Are you anxious about getting that high paying job and buying that new car? Well, your days of scrimping and saving are not quite over. While your new annual salary may be more money than you've ever made, you will have new expenses associated with working and living on your own. Apartment rent, car payments, and living expenses may be familiar to people who have lived off campus, but when you enter the professional ranks your needs and desires change. Preparing now is the best way to avoid financial despair from trying to have it all too soon.

articleTitle: Going for the long term: Increased automation in spacecraft power systems to lengthen the duration of voyages is being developed
abstract: To date Skylab has been the only high power, long duration mission flown by NASA. Launched in 1973, Skylab was designed to operate with a photovoltaic/NiCd battery system providing nominally 8 kW of electrical power to the bus. During the nine month total mission time, up to 10 people (average) were required around the clock to operate the power system.

articleTitle: Art in technology: A photo essay demonstrating the close relationship between art and technology
abstract: Fiber optics, a communications medium in which light signals are transmitted through a fiber of ultra-pure glass. Looking into the soul of this medium, we also find the artistic side of technology. The photography shown on this page and the following two pages is from a traveling exhibition entitled “MicroScapes: The Hidden Art of High Technology.”

articleTitle: The current that kills: Some shocking facts about electricity that deserve notice
abstract: Statistics show that over one thousand people are killed in electrical accidents every year in the United States. Approximately 15 percent of these accidents occur in industry. A larger percentage are electrocuted in the home.

articleTitle: Wanted: Eng. D. degrees: Four undergraduate years are not sufficient to produce a practicing engineer
abstract: The crisis in engineering education is evident. Four years of undergraduate studies are not sufficient to properly educate and produce a practicing engineer. Every report on engineering education, from the Mann report in 1918 to the NSPE (National Society of Professional Engineers) study in 1976, has recommended that certain subjects be added to the engineering curriculum without recommending that any be deleted. The Wickenden report of 1934 entitled “Investigation of Engineering Education, 1923–1929” recommended that more social science and humanities be added to the engineering curriculum. In 1955, the Grinter report recommended that more basic science be added to the curriculum. Recently, ABET (Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology) modified accreditation guidelines to ensure that more engineering design is included in the curriculum. In an article by Cranch and Nordby, industrial spokesmen are quoted as stressing the need to add more communication skills, both oral and written, and management skills to the engineering curriculum.

articleTitle: In pursuit of a space career: Space career options are almost as diverse as the galaxy itself
abstract: From inside the Space Shuttle to the labs of major high-tech corporations and universities, aerospace specialists can be found hard at work. Despite the Challenger tragedy in January of 1986 and the resulting setbacks in the U.S. Space Program, corporate recruiters, government agencies and major aerospace societies are predicting a promising future for those aspiring to aerospace careers.

articleTitle: Surviving in the corporate jungle: Adjusting to your new company's political structure can be more difficult than the job requirements
abstract: You have the grades. You have the talent. You have the drive to succeed. But, getting to the top requires political savvy. Whether you work for a research laboratory, university, or corporation, you will be subjected to on-the-job politics unique to that organization.

articleTitle: Increasing the industrial robot's IQ: Teaching robots to adapt more intelligently to changes in their environment
abstract: The harbinger of the new “mechatronics” age, the industrial robot, was invented in the U.S. in 1961. An industrial robot is a programmable, multi-functional manipulator. It is designed to perform useful work by moving a tool or workpiece through various programmed motions. The principal components of an industrial robot are the manipulator or maneuvering unit, the computer motion controller, and the power unit.

articleTitle: Electronic minds' eyes: Remote sensing and image processing — An eye opening field
abstract: At this moment, as you scan and read this page, you are both “remote sensing” and “image processing.” Remote sensing is the process of acquiring data about a scene from a distance. Image processing is the subsequent correction, feature extraction, and classification of an image. Instinctively, we are familiar with the idea of obtaining a representation of a scene with the eye, and that image then undergoing processing in the brain. Another common sensor is the camera, which captures an image on film or uses a photo-electric detector.

articleTitle: Investing: Questions and answers: The sooner you start the better off you'll be when you need it
abstract: Young professionals just starting out are faced with many important decisions that affect the rest of their lives (Marriage? Move out or live at home? Which car to buy? Accept that out of state job? etc.) At this crucial time individuals should also begin to prepare themselves for their financial future. Financial planning is easily put off because there are many reasons why investments can wait until later. The truth of the matter is with this frame of mind, in 25 years you may be wondering why you procrastinated and find yourself wishing that you knew then what you know now.

articleTitle: The concept of inheritance takes shape: The road to understanding genetic engineering is paved with DNA
abstract: Everything we are is determined by the genetic information we carry. Forays into conquering disease and birth defects depend on understanding genes first. Through the millenia man has known that certain characteristics can be inherited. However, just what and where these genes were remained a mystery until the experiments of Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty (1944) revealed that a polymer called deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was in fact the genetic material responsible.

articleTitle: The F3 systems: A start to time management: Learning to prioritize tasks leads to greater productivity and fulfillment
abstract: So you're about to enter the “real working world?” Great! Just realize, though, that it's tough to spend 100 percent of your time on engineering. Paperwork and other nontechnical tasks can occupy a big chunk of the day leading to frustration and dissatisfaction. However, you can increase your engineering productivity by mastering some simple techniques to handle paperwork and related tasks.

articleTitle: Up, up, and away: Do you have what it takes to make a space-worthy plane?
abstract: A plane that operates efficiently in the air and in space is the current dream of the U.S. Defense Department and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Some of the dream sequences include: flying from New York to Australia in thirty minutes, Tokyo in two hours; reducing the expense of transporting material into space to one tenth the current estimated cost; and the ability to quickly service military space systems. For the U.S. armed forces, particularly the United States Air Force (USAF), this second generation aerospace plane is rapidly becoming a “must have” item. The necessity of having this type of versatile aircraft stems primarily from USAF studies done in 1985 whose findings concluded that a more responsive, less expensive aircraft was needed to complement growing military space activities.

articleTitle: Plug into electric power: Power engineering could be your connection to a high voltage career
abstract: Electrical engineering students face a bewildering array of career options. One of those options, electric power engineering, provides the opportunity to participate in a physically and professionally dynamic environment.

articleTitle: But, where's the orchestra? The inner workings of the machines that have revolutionized the music industry
abstract: During the 1960s a new era began in the field of popular music. The culprit, an instrument that creates sound electronically, is known as the synthesizer. With synthesizers, recording artists cannot only produce new sounds in the studio, but can also reproduce them at a live performance. The advent of the synthesizer opened a whole new world of creativity for composers to explore. Entire string sections could be heard at concerts without extra musicians.

articleTitle: Engineers managing engineers: Technical prowess does not necessarily a good manager make
abstract: College graduation … electrical engineering degree … research position? Not necessarily. Despite the ongoing controversy about the effectiveness of engineers as managers, an increasing number of engineers are successfully pursuing careers in engineering management in today's technically competitive society. For those willing to take the initiative, engineering management can be a lucrative and professionally fulfilling career path.

articleTitle: The plight of software engineers: An examination of people who will have the whole world at their fingertips
abstract: Those of you now preparing to be software engineers will be the architects of computer systems which will profoundly influence life in the early twenty-first century. You will face challenges as large as those that brought us railroads, airplanes, and space travel. And as in all engineering disciplines, acceptable trade-offs will have to be made among economic factors, the laws of nature, and concern for safe and practical end results.

articleTitle: In search of the superemployee: Corporate tests seek the best, brightest, and most productive employees
abstract: After four or more years of constant testing to make the grade, students relish the thought of leaving this annoyance behind as they move into the professional arena. Well, your testing days are not yet over. With employment testing having taken corporate America by storm, don't be surprised if you are asked to submit to psychological, intelligence, honesty, drug and/or genetic tests before a job offer is made.

articleTitle: Logic and functional programming: Fresh concepts in computer processing are revolutionizing modeling needs
abstract: Programming language design amounts to a model, or abstract description, of computation. Most traditional languages are based upon a computational model capable of carrying out arithmetic operations, making variable assignments, calling procedures, looping, and so forth. They are designed to meet the needs of traditionally structured computers. Thus, models of new languages appear to vary only slightly. But times are changing. Ideas about computer processing are breaking new ground and requiring computer languages radically different in their modeling.

articleTitle: Pace conference report: Early involvement in professional issues will net you positive results
abstract: Are you ready for the professional world? Have you wondered what it is like to be a practicing engineer? If you had an all expenses paid trip to Arizona to spend four days with 200 professional engineers, do you think you would get some answers? I know I did. As the IEEE Chairman of the George Washington University Student Branch in Washington, DC, I went with six other student branch chairmen from the Washington area to the 1986 National PACE (Professional Activities Committee for Engineers) Conference. We flew to sunny Phoenix for the Labor Day weekend conference, joining approximately 210 other attendees.

articleTitle: Editorial
abstract: The four-year engineering undergraduate degree is becoming obsolete. The amount of technical material that students need to learn is ever increasing. The growing need to specialize early in the program is contradicted by the push to include more liberal arts and humanities in the curricula. In the process of trying to cram all of it into a four-year program, important labwork and production related courses are often minimal or sacrificed entirely.

articleTitle: Circuit rider branch news
Why stay onboard? Remain state-of-the-art after graduation; maintain your IEEE membership
abstract: IEEE Student membership is an exceptional bargain. A modest amount of money facilitates membership in the professional society that represents the broad area of electrical engineering. Spectrum, The Institute and Potentials provide coverage of the technical and professional progress in the field. Discount student rates for membership in the technical societies allow much deeper reading in specialized areas. Participation in branch, chapter and section activities brings the student into contact with both technical information and a cross section of professional engineers. Access to technical conferences and shows at greatly reduced prices can in itself pay for the cost of membership.

articleTitle: Cover letters can open doors: This important key to a new position is often overlooked
abstract: The campaign for a new job usually begins with a period of prospecting. It is probably the most important activity in an individual's search for a new position.

articleTitle: 1987 Outstanding branch counselors: This year's roster of the facilitators of campus professional activities
abstract: “Thank you so much for all your hard work and dedication, we couldn't have done it without you.” This was the resounding sentiment of winning nominations submitted on behalf of the 1987 Outstanding Branch Counselors and Advisors.

articleTitle: Chairman's corner
abstract: No student needs reminding that electrical engineering in its broadest sense is an extraordinarily complex technical field. Every homework problem and exam reinforces this view. Further, it doesn't take an engineering student long to realize, if only through watching the changes in computers, chips, and instruments, that yesterday's technical breakthrough is today's obsolescent equipment.

articleTitle: Chairman's corner
abstract: It's Fall again, the re-start of the cycle that seems to govern the lives of all of us in the academic world. There are many cycles in the lives of both people and institutions; the academic year is one of the most conspicuous to us.

articleTitle: Chairman's corner
abstract: How can engineers become involved in the issues we see in the world? As individuals, we all take positions of support or opposition. But how can or should engineers, as engineers, involve themselves and their professional organizations? IEEE does this, for example, by adopting position papers on matters within the areas of competence and interest of its membership, and by providing expert assistance to legislative bodies. More to the point, is there a place in branch activities for programs devoted to issues? My answer is, “yes,” with some caution and some work. Awareness of the ethical and social implications of what we do as engineers is an imporant aspect of professional development, and it can lead to popular programs as well. Consider some guidelines that can make such programs viable in a student branch.

articleTitle: Editorial
abstract: As the old saying goes, “All good things must come to an end.” And with this issue of Potentials, my term as Student Editor does just that. It has truly been a rewarding experience for me, and I cannot thanks to some of those who make Potentials a reality; Mary Campbell and Camille Tetta of the IEEE staff; Charles Slivinsky, the hard-working Editor; and the tireless Associate Editor who give freely of their time in order to provide you with a quality publication.

articleTitle: Editorial
abstract: In the previous Editorial, we considered the career of Albert Speer, Hitler's brilliant architect, who ultimately became part and parcel of all that was deplorable about the so-called “Thousand-Year Reich.”

articleTitle: Editorial
abstract: When I responded to the ad for the new student editor of Potentials, I didn't think I had much of a chance. I reasoned, however, that there was no harm in trying. When I found out a few weeks later that I had been chosen, I was excited. And, as I soon found out, I had been given an opportunity to be involved with a very special group of people: the editorial board of Potentials.
